description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de Durango participando en el desafío Guía de supervivencia interplanetaria: mapa marciano. Nuestro objetivo es desarrollar una herramienta interactiva de navegación que utilice coordenadas (latitud y longitud) y datos satelitales de la NASA para trazar las rutas más seguras en Marte, ayudando a los futuros astronautas a esquivar obstáculos topográficos y zonas de alta radiación. ¡Si te apasiona la exploración espacial y únete a nosotros!
summary:
We developed Ares Safe-Route 3D, a real-time multiplayer planetary navigation platform—acting as a survival "Waze" for Mars—that connects a 2D Mission Control Dashboard on PC with multiple 3D first-person (POV) mobile visors for astronauts.
Our prototype addresses the challenge by integrating official NASA MOLA laser altimetry, USGS geological mapping (SIM 3292), and Curiosity rover RAD dosimetry into a multicriteria A* pathfinding engine. Each connected phone operates as an independent astronaut visor moving at a realistic human pace (0.62 m/s), guided by dynamic glowing chevrons projected onto the Martian terrain. The system enables astronauts to place collaborative 3D pins to classify scientific points of interest or hazards, instantly recalculating safe routes for the entire squad during meteorite impacts or solar radiation storms.
This is critical because Mars lacks both GPS satellites and a global magnetosphere; having autonomous, hazard-aware navigation is essential to protect human lives during future extravehicular activities (EVA).
details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

Ares Safe-Route 3D is a real-time distributed planetary navigation platform that functions as a guidance and survival system for extravehicular activities (EVA) on Mars. It connects a Mission Control Base on a computer (featuring a 2D top-down tactical map view) with the mobile phones or tablets of multiple astronauts in real time (featuring a 3D first-person POV):

  • Dynamic per-device registration: The system starts with 0 astronauts, and as each mobile device opens the web link, it automatically registers as a unique, independent explorer (ASTRO_1, ASTRO_2, ASTRO_3...) with its own color and individual route.
  • 3D Visor on the phone: Each astronaut uses two multi-touch virtual joysticks (one to walk at a realistic human speed and another to rotate the view 360°) and follows a line of 45 glowing arrows projected onto the ground (chevrons) that shift from green to coral-orange on turns.
  • Tactical control and hazards on the computer: The operator selects the tablet of any connected astronaut to assign destinations (META, S5, C4, B2, N0, or custom click-to-set waypoints), launch meteorites that sculpt new craters and deactivate nodes trapped inside them, and move solar radiation storms that trigger red proximity alerts on nearby visors.
  • Collaborative 3D Pins: Astronauts place neutral pins on the terrain, and Mission Control classifies them as blue points of interest (informational, without altering routes) or red hazard zones (which instantly recalculate A* paths for the entire squad to bypass them).

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Safety and immediate hazard response: Protects the crew against solar particle events (SPE), falls into steep craters, and meteorite impacts by recalculating safe routes in milliseconds.
  • Cooperative navigation without GPS: Solves the absence of GPS satellites and a global magnetosphere on Mars through relative topographic localization and bidirectional communication between astronauts and the base station.
  • Impact and scalability for future missions: This architecture can be projected directly onto Augmented Reality helmets (AR/HoloLens), connected to spacesuit biometric oxygen sensors to trigger automatic return-to-base routes, dispatch autonomous rovers toward scientific pins of interest, and be adapted to NASA lunar LOLA maps for the Artemis missions or terrestrial rescue teams operating in GPS-denied areas.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Programming languages: Java SE (Java_Grafos_Rutas on port 8081), Python 3 (Python_Calculos_API on port 8080), and TypeScript, HTML5, and CSS (marte-hud on port 4200).
  • Frameworks, libraries, and APIs: Angular, Three.js (WebGLRenderer, 3D Raycaster, and CatmullRomCurve3 splines), native WebSockets (RFC 6455), HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive with TCP_NODELAY, ThreadingHTTPServer, com.sun.net.httpserver, and the Web Speech API for voice alerts.
  • Data structures: HashMap for topographic graph adjacency lists, PriorityQueue for the multicriteria A* heuristic algorithm, Stack and LinkedList for emergency route logs, and a 3D geometry Object Pool to maintain 60 FPS on mobile phones.
  • Official scientific data (NASA / USGS): NASA MGS MOLA laser altimetry mosaic (Mars_MGS_MOLA_DEM_mosaic_global_463m.tif, with real elevations ranging from $-3,242\text{ m}$ to $-3,204\text{ m}$), USGS Geologic Map of Mars (SIM 3292), surface dosimetry series from the Curiosity rover's RAD detector, and MEDA / Boxwork Formations environmental parameters.
  • Hardware and development environment: A computer acting as the central command station, multiple smartphones and tablets connected over a local Wi-Fi network, Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub, and co-engineering assistance with Gemini AI.

How Is Our Project Creative?

  • Intuitive video-game-inspired interface: Replaces hard-to-read coordinates during an emergency with console-style dual-joystick touch controls and dynamic ground-level guide arrows that change color based on terrain curvature.
  • Live interactive physics simulation: Allows the operator to interact directly with the Martian environment by clicking on the map to drop meteorites that deform the topographic mesh and disable nodes in real time, or dragging radiation fronts with the cursor.
  • Dual science and survival management: Integrates geological exploration with tactical safety through tablet-owned 3D pins, distinguishing between scientific discoveries the team can visit and hazards everyone must avoid.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Human physics and biomechanics on Mars: Calibrated movement to the realistic human walking speed in a pressurized spacesuit under Martian gravity ($0.62\text{ m/s}$) using Tobler's hiking function, achieving a steady, natural pace that prevents motion sickness in the visor.
  • Geology and natural shielding: Classified graph nodes according to official USGS lithology, prioritizing firm volcanic basalt plains (lHv, offering $90\%$ topographic shielding and superior traction) over ancient outflow channels (Hto, with $75\%$ shielding) or steep impact craters (AHi).
  • Zero-lag synchronization and session isolation: Implemented a hybrid WebSocket + HTTP Keep-Alive channel, unique per-device identification (UUID), and anti-duplication filters to ensure smooth 60 FPS performance and prevent concurrency conflicts when multiple explorers operate simultaneously.
